findings.claim: The new `mockPrototype !== parent` guard only prevents a *direct* self-cycle; an indirect cycle (where `parent`'s own prototype chain already contains `mockPrototype`) still throws `TypeError: Cyclic __proto__ value`.
findings.rationale: `Object.setPrototypeOf` rejects any assignment that would create a cycle, not just `setPrototypeOf(o, o)`. If an implementation is a subclass whose `prototype` chain passes through `mockPrototype` (realistic when a mock is used as a base class, or when a mocked class's prototype was previously reparented onto this mock), `mockPrototype !== parent` is true and `Object.getPrototypeOf(mockPrototype) !== parent` is true, so the code still calls `setPrototypeOf` and throws. A chain walk (`let p = parent; while (p) { if (p === mockPrototype) return; p = Object.getPrototypeOf(p) }`) or a try/catch would cover the general case. Moderate confidence this is reachable in practice; high confidence the guard is incomplete in principle.

findings.claim: When `mockPrototype === parent`, the function now silently leaves the previous prototype in place instead of reverting the chain, so a stale parent from an earlier implementation can leak.
findings.rationale: The comment directly above states the invariant that an implementation without a usable prototype reverts the chain to `Object.prototype`. With the new guard, the self-referential case takes the early-skip path and keeps whatever parent a *previous* `mockImplementation` installed, rather than resetting to `Object.prototype`. If the goal is only to avoid the TypeError, the safer behavior is likely `Object.setPrototypeOf(mockPrototype, Object.prototype)` in that branch. Medium confidence — depends on whether the self-referential case is ever reached after a prior non-trivial implementation.

findings.claim: `parent` is still not validated as object-or-null, so a non-object `.prototype` (e.g. `fn.prototype = 42`) reaches `Object.setPrototypeOf` and throws a `TypeError`.
findings.rationale: `(implementation as Constructable | undefined)?.prototype ?? Object.prototype` only defends against `null`/`undefined`. A function whose `prototype` has been assigned a primitive yields a primitive `parent`; `Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, 42)` throws TypeError. Pre-existing rather than introduced by this hunk, but since the change is specifically hardening this call site it is worth covering here. Low-to-medium confidence that it matters in practice.
